content: Moxibustion is a therapeutic practice rooted in traditional East Asian medicine that involves the use of moxa, a substance derived from the mugwort herb. This technique is integral to the medical traditions of countries such as China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Tibet, and Mongolia. The mugwort is typically aged and ground into a fine, fluffy material, which is then either burned directly or processed into a stick resembling a cigar, though it is not intended for smoking. Practitioners may apply moxa indirectly, often in conjunction with acupuncture needles, or occasionally burn it directly on the patient’s skin. The term moxa originates from the Japanese word mogusa (艾), where the u is softly pronounced. In Japan, the herb is also referred to as yomogi (蓬). In Chinese, the same character is used but pronounced as ài or àiróng (艾絨), which translates to velvet of ài. The Chinese character for moxa is a component of the term zhēnjiǔ (針灸), which is commonly translated as acupuncture. Moxibustion is employed to warm specific regions or acupuncture points on the body, with the goal of enhancing circulation and promoting a smoother flow of blood and qi (vital energy). Research has indicated that mugwort possesses emmenagogue properties, meaning it can stimulate blood flow in the pelvic region and uterus. It is also believed that moxibustion can counteract cold and dampness within the body and is sometimes used to assist in turning breech babies during pregnancy. Historically, moxibustion is thought to have preceded acupuncture, with the latter being introduced as a complementary technique after the 2nd century BCE. Different schools of acupuncture incorporate moxibustion to varying extents. For instance, practitioners of the Five-Element acupuncture tradition may apply moxa directly to the skin, while those trained in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) often use moxa rolls held above the treatment area. To prevent scarring, moxa can also be burned on top of a thin slice of ginger root. Moxibustion is particularly valued for addressing chronic conditions, states of deficiency (such as general weakness), and age-related health issues. Bian Que, a renowned and semi-legendary physician from ancient China (circa 500 BCE), was an early advocate of moxibustion. In his writings, he emphasized the superiority of moxa over acupuncture in certain cases, arguing that moxa could replenish the body’s energy and treat both excess and deficient conditions. Conversely, he cautioned against using acupuncture on patients with significant deficiencies, as the manipulation of needles could deplete their energy further. A classical text, Gao Huang Shu (膏肓俞), is dedicated entirely to the therapeutic applications of moxibustion on a single acupuncture point. Additionally, Taoist practitioners have historically combined scarring moxibustion with Chinese medical astrology as part of their longevity practices. Depending on the desired direction of qi flow, practitioners may also use acupuncture needles made from various materials in conjunction with moxa. Beyond its medical applications, mugwort has been revered in other cultural contexts. Indigenous peoples in North and South America consider mugwort a sacred plant used for divination, spiritual healing, and as a general remedy. Mugwort, along with other herbs, was often tied into smudge sticks for ceremonial purposes. In Europe, sprigs of mugwort were placed under pillows to induce vivid dreams, and the herb was associated with magical practices during the Anglo-Saxon era.
